say.text: A fire victim comes in after a fire in a closed room. Headache and confusion for two hours.
The pulse oximeter reads 98%. What is your next step?

choices.label: Reassure, since the saturation is normal
Send serum lactate to look for cyanide
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Co-oximetry measures carboxyhaemoglobin directly, so it gives the CO load that a normal saturation hides.
Pulse oximetry reads falsely normal in CO poisoning, so the number cannot settle the question.
Tempting: a comfortable patient with a 98% reading looks well oxygenated.
But the oximeter cannot tell carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin, so a normal number does not exclude CO.
Send co-oximetry for the carboxyhaemoglobin level, which measures the CO load directly.

sure_note.text: You were sure the number settled it. That is the favoured exam trap: a falsely normal oximeter in CO poisoning.

say.text: Tempting: smoke sends you to cyanide, and lactate is the marker people reach for.
But lactate is a cyanide clue, raised with unexplained lactic acidosis or shock, and it does not measure carboxyhaemoglobin.
With headache and confusion, the CO question comes first: send carboxyhaemoglobin by co-oximetry.

sure_note.text: You were sure the smoke meant cyanide. Keep the split: CO comes first with headache and confusion, and cyanide needs its own clue.

say.text: Ask which result measures the poison itself, rather than a reading that can look normal.
The oximeter reads 98% in a smoke victim whose carboxyhaemoglobin is high.
What is the probe actually doing?

choices.label: Saturation is truly normal, so delivery is too
It cannot tell carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin
Dissolved oxygen makes up the lost capacity
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. It cannot separate the two haemoglobins, so a normal reading says nothing about the CO load.
Co-oximetry measures the carboxyhaemoglobin directly, so it is the test that shows the real figure.
Think of the oximeter as a judge that sees red but not which red.
Tempting: a normal number feels like proof that the blood is carrying enough oxygen.
But the probe cannot tell carboxyhaemoglobin apart, so the reading can look normal while the blood carries little oxygen.
Co-oximetry gives the carboxyhaemoglobin level, which is the number that matters here.

sure_note.text: You were sure the reading meant normal delivery. Hold on to it: a falsely normal oximeter in CO is a favoured trap.

say.text: Tempting: plasma oxygen sounds like a backup when haemoglobin falls short.
But that is not why the probe misreads: it cannot tell carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin.
Co-oximetry shows the carboxyhaemoglobin level, so you can see the lost capacity directly.

sure_note.text: You were sure of the plasma backup. The error sits in the probe's number, not in the plasma.

say.text: Ask whether the probe can tell the two kinds of haemoglobin apart, and what the blood is really carrying.
A man is burned in a room fire. Soot is in his mouth, his nasal hair is singed and his voice is hoarse.
Which test confirms inhalation injury?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Bronchoscopy looks straight at the airway below the cords and shows soot, oedema or erythema.
Those findings are the injury itself, so direct vision is the confirming test.
Tempting: a chest film is the routine first image on a burns ward, so it feels like the check.
But the X-ray is often normal early, so a clear film cannot rule out airway injury.
Bronchoscopy looks at the airway itself, which is the test that confirms the injury.

sure_note.text: You were sure a film would settle it. A normal early X-ray is the trap: it reassures and misleads.

say.text: Tempting: a blood gas measures oxygenation, so it feels like a test of lung injury.
But an arterial gas reads gas exchange and carboxyhaemoglobin, not the airway itself.
Bronchoscopy shows the soot, oedema or erythema below the cords, which the gas cannot show.

sure_note.text: You were sure a gas would show the injury. The gas measures the blood; the injury sits in the airway.

say.text: Ask which test looks at the airway itself, rather than at the blood or the chest outline.
A fire victim with soot in the mouth has a normal chest X-ray on arrival, and is hoarse.
What does the film tell you?

choices.label: Clear film excludes it, so no airway concern follows
A normal film does not exclude it; bronchoscope the airway
Repeat the film at six hours before any airway decision
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. An early film is often normal, so a clear one cannot rule out airway injury.
Bronchoscopy looks at the airway directly, which is why it is the test that confirms the injury.
Tempting: a clear film feels like clearance, and the patient looks settled.
But the film is often normal early, so it cannot exclude airway injury.
Bronchoscopy shows soot, oedema or erythema directly, so that is the test to order.

sure_note.text: You were sure the film cleared the airway. It is the same error as the first X-ray, in a new form.

say.text: Tempting: repeating a film sounds careful and cautious.
But a repeat film is still a chest film, and it does not look at the airway.
Bronchoscopy answers the question now, rather than after another film.

sure_note.text: You were sure waiting was careful. Waiting on a film delays the test that answers the question.

say.text: Ask how much of the airway a chest film can show, and which test looks inside it.
Smoke from burning plastics. The patient is in shock, with lactic acidosis that nothing else explains.
Which antidote do you give?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Burning plastics with unexplained lactic acidosis or shock points to cyanide.
Hydroxocobalamin is the cyanide antidote, so it is the treatment here.
Tempting: one fire gives both poisons, so one oxygen treatment looks like it covers the smoke.
But 100% oxygen treats CO, and this picture is lactic acidosis, which is the cyanide clue.
Give hydroxocobalamin for cyanide. Oxygen belongs to the CO question.

sure_note.text: You were sure one oxygen treatment covered both. CO and cyanide get different antidotes.

say.text: Partly right: hyperbaric oxygen is used for CO, but in selected cases, so it is not the first measure here.
This picture points to cyanide, and the cyanide antidote is hydroxocobalamin.
Ask which poison the lactic acidosis points to, then which antidote belongs to that poison.
Match each poison to its treatment in smoke inhalation.
Which pairing is right?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. 100% oxygen treats carbon monoxide, and hydroxocobalamin treats cyanide.
Hydrofluoric acid is a different poison again, and its antidote is calcium gluconate.
Use the clue to pick the poison first, then the antidote that belongs to it.
Tempting: the same smoke makes the two poisons look interchangeable, so the labels seem to swap.
But the antidotes are swapped: oxygen goes with CO, and hydroxocobalamin with cyanide.
Use the clue first: lactic acidosis points to cyanide, while headache and confusion point to CO.

sure_note.text: You were sure the labels could swap. Pairing each poison with its antidote is the recall point.

say.text: Tempting: one oxygen treatment for everything sounds simple after a fire.
But 100% oxygen is for CO, and cyanide needs hydroxocobalamin, not oxygen.
Cyanide suspicion comes from lactic acidosis or shock, so it gets its own antidote.

sure_note.text: You were sure one treatment covered both poisons. It does not; each poison has its own antidote.

say.text: Start with the clue for each poison, then pick the antidote that matches that clue.
